question: The 1977 murder of Arturo Ruiz is one of the many violations of the right to truth and justice during Spain’s transition to democracy. Reports of collaboration between far-right and state forces require transparency. Despite the Democratic Memory Law and the European Commission’s recommendations in its Rule of Law Report to improve access to information, declassification of official documents remains an obstacle. In view of the above: 1.

What does the Commission make of the Spanish state’s failure to follow its recommendation in the 2022, 2023 and 2024 Rule of Law Reports with regard to improving access to information, specifically in relation to the Arturo Ruiz and similar cases?
In the Commission’s view, does the refusal to declassify documents on human rights violations during the Spanish transition to democracy breach EU rules on access to official documents?
What measures can the Commission propose to ensure the families of victims like Arturo Ruiz can exercise their right to truth and justice in line with the principles of the rule of law in the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.2.2025) In the Spanish chapter of the 2024 Rule of Law Report1, the Commission noted that, in October 2023, Spain ratified the Council of Europe’s Convention on Access to Public Documents, which recognises a general right of access to official documents held by public authorities.

The report also informed that the Spanish government intends to re-launch the adoption of the draft law on official secrets and thus recommended Spain to advance with this adoption. The Commission will continue to assess developments pertaining to media freedom and pluralism in all Member States, including Spain, in the context of the preparation of the 2025 Rule of Law Report.

The Commission considers that safeguarding the common memory of crimes of totalitarian and authoritarian regimes, as well as transition to democracy, is essential to safeguarding EU values of human dignity, fundamental rights, rule of law and democracy for current and future generations. However, it should be recalled that remembrance policies are under the competence of Member States.

The Commission remains committed to taking all necessary measures to ensure compliance with EU law and upholding the rule of law in all Member States and will continue to work with the Spanish authorities to promote the rule of law. More generally, same as for all the Member States, the Commission follows rule of law developments in Spain under the annual Rule of Law Cycle and its report.
